summary: The paper is a measurement and data-construction study, not a causal or regression paper. It reports no regression estimates, so the usual robustness machinery (alternative controls, placebo tests, subsample estimates) does not apply. The robustness-relevant material is the pilot validation of the LLM against human coders, the full-run counts, the housing-listing descriptives, and two descriptive subgroup or pattern claims. The audit found nine issues. (1) The headline claim that LLM–human agreement matches human–human agreement is stated without the paper's own caveat that the 34-article pilot, with 3 relevant articles, can only be indicative. (2) The agreement figures are computed after "unclear" and truncated-text articles are recoded as not relevant, and no alternative treatment is shown. (3) The prompt was revised after the first run and the reported agreement comes from a re-run on the same validation set, with no pre-revision results. (4) Run-to-run consistency is reported only for relevance, not for dates. (5) No sensitivity to model, reasoning level or temperature is reported. (6) The pilot validation is extended to the 3,187-article full run without any check on the full run. (7) The claim that date precision depends on attention rests on an unadjusted 17/18 vs 2/26 comparison. (8) The seasonal-clustering claim has no reported monthly counts. (9) The Appendix A.3.2 classification rule ("first type in the table") contradicts its own example. The appendix text also says the 2024 gap in the listing data runs from January to April, while the body sentence says only Q1 2024 is missing. Table CSV/markdown objects were not used as evidence, following parser-quality guidance; all quotes come from page text.

findings.finding_summary: The abstract, introduction and conclusion state that LLM–human relevance agreement equals human–human agreement (97 percent), without the Section 4 caveat that 34 articles with 3 relevant ones cannot test whether the rates differ and that results are indicative only.

location.text_quote: the same rate as between two human coders

findings.claim_text: On the pilot, the LLM agrees with a human coder on the relevance of 97 percent of the articles, the same rate as between two human coders.
findings.evidence_summary: Tables 3 and 4 both show 33 of 34 agreements, and the single disagreement is the same Stord article in both. Section 4 states the sample 'is too small to test whether the two agreement rates differ' and that results are 'indicative only'. Section 8 repeats that with three relevant articles the difference cannot be tested. The abstract, the introduction ('very close to the rate between the two human coders') and the conclusion ('matched human–human agreement') omit this limit. Agreement is also driven by 30 not-relevant articles in a sample where only 3 are relevant, and no chance-corrected agreement or uncertainty interval is reported. The caveat exists in the body but is not carried into the headline claims.

findings.finding_summary: Run-to-run consistency is reported only for the relevance decision on 34 articles. No consistency is reported for the extracted opening dates, which are the paper's central output. Which run's date is compared with the human coder is also not stated.

findings.evidence_summary: Section 3.2 says the three-run consistency check concerns 'the first-stage coding (relevant vs. not relevant)' and that one of 34 articles (3%) disagreed across runs. Table 4 uses the majority of the three runs for relevance. For dates, Section 4.2 compares the LLM date with the pilot coder on three articles. It does not say whether the date comes from a single run, a majority, or a consensus, nor whether the three runs gave the same date and precision. The date comparison is also conditional on articles both coders coded as relevant, so it cannot reflect date errors in articles missed or wrongly included. The abstract's 'gives the same opening date for all three relevant articles' rests on this unreported stability.

The reasoning level is 'low' and the temperature is left at its default. No result from another model or setting is shown, and the validation covers one model-setting combination on 34 articles. The central results (92 articles, 43 projects, 29 dated) depend on this single configuration. The paper presents this as an exploratory pipeline, so the gap is a limitation to state, not a necessary extra analysis.

findings.finding_summary: The pilot validation (34 articles, 3 relevant) is the only accuracy evidence, yet the abstract and conclusion present the full-run counts (92 articles, 43 projects, 29 dated) as pipeline output. The full run has no human check, and its pilot-versus-full-run composition differs sharply.

findings.evidence_summary: Section 8 acknowledges that a random sample from the 3,187-article run still needs checking against human coding, so no precision, recall or date accuracy is available for the full run. The pilot differs from the full run: in the pilot, 6 of 34 articles (about 18 percent) were unclear mainly from missing or very short text, while Table 6 reports 2 'Unclear' of 3,187. The pilot searched one term ('sykkelvei') over about six weeks, and the full-run search term and prompt version are not stated. The wider-relevance prompt change was not tested in the pilot, which only covered cycling-path articles. The abstract and conclusion report the full-run counts without a statement that they are unvalidated. The limitation appears only in Next Steps, and the project grouping and date precision were done by hand.

findings.finding_summary: Section 6.3 infers that date precision 'is not random but depends on how much attention an opening receives' from an unadjusted comparison (17 of 18 projects with a ceremony dated to the day, versus 2 of 26 without), with no control for project size or the way ceremony coverage is defined.

location.text_quote: This suggests that the precision of the dates is not random but

findings.claim_text: This suggests that the precision of the dates is not random but depends on how much attention an opening receives.
findings.evidence_summary: The paper gives direct subgroup counts: 18 projects with a reported ceremony, of which 17 are day-dated, and 2 of 26 day-dated without one. This is a descriptive contrast and no test is reported. The same section later proposes model (1) with project characteristics such as length and cost to test the relationship. The sentence 'This suggests' is hedged, but it supports the conclusion that dates are non-randomly missing, which motivates restricting model (2) to precisely dated projects. Ceremony and date precision are both read from the same articles. Articles reporting a ceremony naturally state a date, so the association could arise from reporting rather than attention, and size or project type is uncontrolled. The paper itself notes that model (1) should be estimated first.

findings.finding_summary: The claim that openings 'cluster before winter and summer holidays' is stated without any reported monthly or quarterly counts. It is based on shares of relevant articles by publication month, from 92 articles, with few July–August articles in the extraction.

location.text_quote: This indicates that openings cluster before winter and summer

findings.claim_text: October–December 2025 and May–June 2026 have the highest share of relevant articles, and February–April 2026 the lowest. This indicates that openings cluster before winter and summer holidays.
findings.cannot_verify_reason: No table or figure reports monthly counts or shares of relevant articles, so the seasonal pattern cannot be checked.
findings.evidence_summary: The paragraph after Table 6 describes the highest and lowest shares by period, but no table, figure or counts show the monthly data. Table 6 gives only totals (92 relevant articles; 43 projects). The shares are of relevant articles by publication date, not of openings by opening date, and the paper itself notes that the archive has few July–August 2026 articles. Under 100 relevant articles are spread over 13 months, and the date-precision breakdown shows only 19 projects dated to the day. The inference from article-publication shares to openings clustering is therefore not supported by any reported evidence. The same paragraph ranks counties ('Most projects are found in Nordland county') without counts.

findings.evidence_summary: Table 9, read from the page-18 text, lists Parking & storage (including “stativ”) before Infrastructure (including “bysykkel”). Applying the stated first-type rule, 'bysykkelstativ' would be Parking & storage. The text instead assigns it to Infrastructure. The stated rule and the example cannot both describe the implemented classification. The author describes the classification as coarse with likely misclassifications. The effect on Table 8 is bounded: Figure 2 gives 'bysykkelstativ' at 0.5 percent of listings, and Infrastructure leads Parking & storage by 2.6 points in Table 8, so the ranking is unlikely to change. The inconsistency matters for reproducibility of the type shares.

notes: No regression-based robustness claims, pre-analysis plan, or promised robustness checks exist in the manuscript. 'Robust' language does not appear. Equivalent claims ('the same rate', 'matched', 'persists', 'differences across the country') were inventoried and reconciled against Tables 3-4, Section 3.2 and Section 6.3.
Table CSV/markdown objects were not used as evidence, per the parser-quality guidance. All quotes come from page text files. Figure 3 series values are in graphics and were not recovered.
County differences in listing mentions (Figure 4) and the Table 7 shares are descriptive and not interpreted causally, so no finding was raised on them.
